newsitem.title: MEXICO: Ruling party rebels against Zedillo over key reform.
newsitem.headline: Ruling party rebels against Zedillo over key reform.

text.p: A rare rebellion by ruling party legislators against President Ernesto Zedillo shows that hardliners in his party are determined not to surrender their 67-year grip on power, opposition legislators said on Thursday.

Deputies from Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) changed during a debate on Wednesday key clauses of an electoral reform bill to open up Mexico's political system and give opposition parties a fairer chance of winning elections.

The PRI deputies' rebellion tore up parts of an accord painstakingly negotiated over months with the main opposition parties and sent by Zedillo to the normally compliant Chamber of Deputies, where the PRI has a large majority.

"This is a blow to Ernesto Zedillo," said Alejandro Gonzalez Alcocer, a deputy for the right-wing PAN opposition party. "The hardline group of "dinosaurs" in the PRI are trying to stop (reform) at all costs".
For the main left-wing opposition party, the PRD, deputy Graco Ramirez described the PRI's about-face as "a vote of fear, fear of democracy".
PRI deputies were in defiant mood on Thursday as the Chamber of Deputies debated the bill's second and final reading. A vote was expected late on Thursday.
"This is not a matter for the president of the republic", said PRI legislator Jorge Moreno. "This is what we want".

Such fighting talk is common in countries with more independent legislatures but almost unheard of from the PRI, created after the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution to serve as the institutional arm of the all-powerful presidency.

Moreno, like other PRI legislators, admitted his party had been upset by heavy losses in town hall elections last Sunday and feared it might lose its 67-year majority in Congress when Mexico elects legislators next July.
Among the most important changes, the PRI altered the electoral reform bill so that:
-- exceeding campaign spending limits would no longer be an electoral offence, only an "administrative error"
-- coalitions between opposition parties would be severely restricted
-- plans for a special body to audit party finances in campaigns would be scrapped.
There was no immediate reaction from Zedillo, who was visiting Argentina when the deputies launched their rebellion.
